outcome: The general Zilber-Pink conjecture remains open, but several genuine restricted cases were proven in the window: Dogra (self-products of curves with degenerate reduction, submitted Mar 2024), Daw-Orr (curves in Y(1)^n under multiplicative degeneration — published in Duke Math. J. Sept 2025, though first posted to arXiv in 2022), Klingler-Tayou (subvarieties not defined over Q-bar, Apr 2025), and Daw-Orr-Papas (further cases in Y(1)^3, Oct 2025). No AI system produced or contributed to any of these results; the only AI-related touchpoint is a Jan 2026 GitHub issue requesting a Lean formalization of the conjecture's statement, with no proof attempt.
summary: The Zilber-Pink conjecture (finiteness of atypical/maximal atypical subvarieties in a mixed Shimura variety or semiabelian variety) is a broad unifying conjecture in unlikely intersections theory, and it remains open in general as of September 2026 — the Wikipedia article on it (last touched 7 Nov 2025) still describes it as 'wide open' with only special cases proven, which matches what I found independently. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 to today), several genuine restricted cases were proved, each narrowing (not varying) the stated question by restricting the class of X or V, which under the deep-dive's §3.1 rule makes each a 'case of the problem' rather than a related/variant problem: (1) Netan Dogra, arXiv:2403.05481, submitted 8 March 2024 (v1; a v3 was posted 7 July 2026, well within the window), proves Zilber-Pink for n-fold self-products of a curve inside the self-product of its Jacobian under degenerate-reduction and no-extra-endomorphism hypotheses, for n sufficiently small. (2) Christopher Daw and Martin Orr's paper on curves in a product of modular curves under multiplicative degeneration was first posted to arXiv in August 2022 (predating the window) but was formally published in the Duke Mathematical Journal (vol. 174, no. 13, pp. 2877-2926) on 15 September 2025 — I confirmed this date directly via Project Euclid. Per §6.3, I date the underlying event by first written argument (2022, out of window) but the paper was actively revised inside the window (v2 Apr 2024, v3 Jan 2025, v4 Mar 2025) and only reached expert-vetted journal form in Sept 2025; I treat the Duke publication as the in-window event supporting a 'partial' status rather than 'open_stale', since a careful reader in Jan 2024 would not yet have had the peer-reviewed, final-form result. (3) Klingler and Tayou, arXiv:2504.00865 (submitted 1 April 2025), prove Zilber-Pink for subvarieties of mixed Shimura varieties not defined over the algebraic closure of Q in a strong sense, plus an analogous VHS statement. (4) Daw, Orr and Papas, arXiv:2510.09603 (submitted 10 October 2025, revised Feb 2026), extend the Y(1)^n line of results to further cases in Y(1)^3. I independently verified all submission dates, abstracts, and the Duke publication date by opening the arXiv abstract pages and the Project Euclid record directly (not relying on the triage's dates or notes). None of the four papers, nor any of the other in-window papers found (Barroero-Dill on distinguished categories, Bhatta on PEL types, Pila on Schanuel+Zilber-Pink, Daw's June 2025 survey, etc.), show any AI/ML involvement in the mathematics — no acknowledgement, method section, or abstract mentions a language model, automated theorem prover, or AI-assisted search, in what full-text I could access (extraction was degraded for three of the four PDFs, so absence-of-mention confidence is high but not absolute for those). The one AI-related touchpoint found anywhere near this conjecture is GitHub issue #1824 in DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository, opened 21 January 2026, titled 'Zilber-Pink Conjecture', which asks contributors to formalize the conjecture's *statement* in Lean 4/Mathlib (rated difficulty 4/5, tagged needs-prerequisites, still open and unassigned as of the check). This is not a proof attempt, a bound, or any mathematical contribution — it is an infrastructure request so that AI theorem-provers could eventually be pointed at the problem — so it does not change ai_role from none for the mathematical progress itself; I mention it here rather than assigning it its own event because it produced no mathematical result. I classify the overall status as 'partial' (a case of the problem settled) rather than 'progress' or 'open', because multiple genuine special cases were proved with a clear direction of confirmation (the finiteness statement was proved, not refuted, in each restricted setting), and rather than 'resolved' or 'claimed' because the general conjecture named in the Wikipedia bullet is untouched.
competing_reading: One could argue for 'open' with no_change_found if one reads the Wikipedia bullet as asking only about the fully general statement over arbitrary mixed Shimura/semiabelian varieties with no restriction — under a very strict reading, none of the four papers touch 'the conjecture' itself, only proper sub-cases, and an observer could say nothing changed about the open problem as such. I reject this reading because §3.1 explicitly says a case obtained by restricting the stated question counts, normally as partial, and that is exactly the shape of all four results (restricting X, restricting V, or restricting the field of definition). A second competing reading concerns the Daw-Orr paper's date: one could argue for 'open_stale' since the underlying mathematical result was already known (posted to arXiv) before 26 January 2024, and only the journal's peer-reviewed publication happened in the window — under that reading the paper would not represent a new event at all, just a formality. I lean toward 'partial' with the Duke publication as a supporting (not primary) event because the paper underwent substantive revision within the window and its expert-vetted, citable form only existed from September 2025.
what_would_settle_it: Full text access to the acknowledgements sections of the Daw-Orr, Daw-Orr-Papas, and Dogra papers (PDF extraction was degraded) would firm up the 'no AI involvement' finding to high confidence. A check of whether GitHub issue #1824 has since been formalized or closed would clarify whether the AI-formalization effort progressed beyond a stub request.

judgement.doubts: The researcher's argument that the Daw-Orr Duke publication is an in-window event is wrong under F7: its first written argument is August 2022, so it is pre-snapshot and cannot set the status. This does not change the code, since three post-snapshot case results (Dogra, Klingler-Tayou, Daw-Orr-Papas) each support partial on their own. Daw and Orr stay in credited_humans through Daw-Orr-Papas.
